study.title: Psalm 81 - hear the voice of God and receive its abundance
study.overview: This psalm unites an invitation to celebration and solemn warning. First, he calls the people to praise God with music and joy in the feasts marked by Him. Then he recalls the deliverance of Egypt and the provision of God in the wilderness as the basis of the covenant. Then the Lord himself speaks to the people, laments their disobedience and shows the consequences of rejecting their voice. Finally, it closes with a promise: if the people hear it, they will have victory over the enemies, and they will be sustained with abundance.

outline.title: Invitation to praise with music
outline.explanation: The psalm begins by calling on Israel to celebrate God with singing, instruments and joy. Worship is not silent or improvised; it involves the assembled people, celebrating the strength that comes from the Lord.

outline.title: The Feast as Remembrance of Liberation
outline.explanation: The celebration is presented as the statute and order of God. The psalmist recalls the departure of Egypt, the relief of the burden, and the divine provision in the time of anguish, including the test in the waters of Meribah.

outline.title: The call to listen and the tragedy of rebellion
outline.explanation: God speaks directly to his people, demanding attention to his voice and exclusive fidelity. But Israel would not hear him; then he was left to the desires of his own heart and his own counsels.

outline.title: Divine lament and promise of restoration
outline.explanation: The Lord expresses the desire for the people to walk in their ways. If this happened, the enemies would be defeated and the people would be sustained with abundant wheat and honey from the rock.

study.context: The notes provided connect the psalm to a liturgical celebration, possibly the feast of the trumpets or the other festive occasion marked by the cult. The text presents the psalm as a song for a public assembly, with the use of instruments and response of the people. This background reinforces that the feast was not only religious emotion, but a moment to remember the covenant, listen to God's instruction and renew obedience.
study.theology: The theological center of the psalm is that God is at the same time the liberator and the legislator of his people. He is the strength of Israel, the one who brought him out of Egypt, heard his cry and sustained him in the wilderness. Therefore, true worship cannot be separated from obedience. The psalm shows that idolatry is not only ritual error, but relational rejection of the voice of God. It also teaches that disobedience brings a judgment often expressed in the form of abandonment to one's own desires. At the same time, the final promise reveals the goodness of God: if the people hear, He defeats the enemies and feeds them generously. The abundance of wheat and the honey of the rock are images of abundant provision, not of human merit, but of the grace of the Lord for a faithful people.

scholarViews.insight: The notes point out that God pleads with his people to remember the covenant and commandments, especially in the call to hear his voice and obey.
The note understands the psalm as appropriate for a solemnity of worship, destined both to praise God and to instruct the people in worship.
Observation on the end of the psalm understands the expression of abundance as a fed upward provision of wheat, with also spiritual reading in some ancient interpreters.

questions: What changes in our worship when we remember that singing is also an act of obedience to the covenant of God?
In which areas does God's people today run the risk of hearing their voice less and more the counsels themselves?
How can the remembrance of the past deliverance strengthen confidence in God's future provision?
study.practice: Set a moment to turn praise into memory and commitment. When praying, explicitly recall a deliverance that God has already accomplished in his life and ask him to align his desires at his will. Then choose a concrete area in which you have resisted God's voice and take a visible step of obedience this week. If possible, practice praise in community, not just as emotion, but as an answer to the Word heard.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not allow to define with certainty which specific party is in view throughout the psalm; therefore, any most accurate historical identification should be treated with caution. There is also mention, in Adam Clarke's notes, of ancient readings and spiritual applications about verse 16; this is interpretative and should not be presented as unique and definitive meaning of the text.
